• Origin: Asia
  • Height: 15-30+ cm
  • Width: 10-20 cm
  • Light demand: Medium
  • CO2: Low

• Common name: Water Sprite
  • Other names: Indian Fern, Indian Water Fern, Fine Leaf Indian Fern, Water Horn Fern, Water Stag-horn Fern, Mizuwarabi
  • Difficulty: Easy
  • Lighting: moderate to high
  • Water hardness: soft to hard
  • Substrate: any, or floating
  • Growth rate: fast
  • Grows submersed and emersed
  • Placement: mid- to background
  • Height: up to 30 cm and more
  • CO2: not needed to low
  • Propagation: adventitious plantlets / cuttings

Ceratopteris thalictroides inhabits tropical regions on almost all continents. It is hardy, versatile and well adapted to a wide range of habitats. It is found mainly in swampy areas, swamp forests, irrigation ponds and ditches, taro patches, rice paddies, marshes, and still and slow-moving water bodies.

It shows a degree of seasonality, reaching maturity and shedding spores in the dry season. Unlike other ferns such as Java fern, Water Sprite thrives in sunny to partially shaded water.
Do not try it in nano tanks: even one plant will overrun the tank. The recommended minimum is a 40-litre tank. A larger tank is ideal, since it grows very fast and big.

• Dương xỉ nước trồng ở hậu cảnh, trung cảnh hay thả nổi đều được. Lá nó xẻ nhánh mảnh, đặt cạnh những cây có dáng lá khác thì nhìn tương phản rõ.
  • Với bể có phần cây mọc trên cạn, nó trồng ở phía sau, đúng chỗ chuyển từ phần dưới nước lên phần trên cạn. Cây vươn khỏi mặt nước được thì tốt, không thì cũng không sao.
  • Trong bể nhỏ để hở mặt, cây có thể vươn lên khỏi mặt nước và ra những lá cạn rất đẹp.
  • Loài này mọc nhanh nên phải cắt tỉa thường xuyên.

Ceratopteris thalictroides is a pantropical fern, 15-30 cm high and 10-20 cm wide. This plant normally grows fast, but the addition of CO2 may be necessary to promote growth. In small, open aquariums, it can grow out of the tank and form beautiful surface leaves.

Water Sprite is easy to maintain and needs minimal care. It grows fast and covers a large area quickly, so trim the stems from time to time, but do not trim the main stem that emerges from the roots. After trimming, remove the stems for disposal or planting in another tank. Because it grows rapidly and uses up many nutrients, fertilisation may be needed to avoid deficiencies.

Planting: plant healthy plants deep in 5–7 cm of gravel or sand. Dig a small hole, place the plant and anchor the roots with small rocks, otherwise it will float out. Do not completely bury the roots, as new growth starts at the base of the plant. Handle gently, as roots and stems are tender. It can also be attached to porous surfaces such as lava rock or driftwood.

Floating: it can also be floated on the surface. After a few days it sprouts hanging roots that absorb nutrients. Floating plants grow taller with wider, flatter leaves, whereas rooted plants are very ferny and delicate. The thin roots trap edible matter and make a good foraging ground for shrimp. The long roots attach to decor, so bear this in mind when placing it.

Propagation: it propagates through adventitious plantlets that break off and root in the substrate or water column; remove excess plantlets to prevent overcrowding. It can also be propagated by cutting mature stems with many healthy leaves and planting them. It also reproduces by spores, but this is not viable in an aquarium.

Water Sprite is a relatively hardy plant and tolerates most water conditions once healthy and established.

Temperature: 22–27°C for proper growth. Below 20°C, growth slows significantly and leaves become smaller.

pH: 6.0–8.0; it also tolerates 5.5–8 well.

Hardness: it generally does not care, but for optimal growth keep 2–15 GH and 3–8 KH.

Water flow: it thrives in still and slow-moving water. Keep it away from fast currents and direct flow, which damage the plant.

Lighting: medium to high. It grows slower in low light and faster in high light, and its growth and appearance vary with light and other conditions.

Substrate: the root system is tender and brittle, so soil, coarse sand or fine gravel is most suitable.

Supplements: CO2 and fertilisers are usually not needed for healthy growth, but adding them significantly increases the growth rate. In shrimp tanks, high CO2 and copper (found in most fertilisers) are extremely dangerous to shrimp, so use shrimp-safe fertilisers.

The finely branched leaves are very decorative and provide good contrast to other leaf shapes. In good light Ceratopteris thalictroides grows fast and helps prevent algae by consuming large amounts of nutrients. This makes it a good starter plant in small aquariums.

The genus Ceratopteris is derived from the Greek "keras, keratos" (horn) and "pteris" (fern), referring to the foliage. The species name "thalictroides" means the leaves resemble those of the genus Thalictrum.

The genus was described by Brongniart in 1821. Species recognition has been confused because of high polymorphism. In 1974 Lloyd combined eleven species into four: Ceratopteris cornuta, C. pteridoides, C. richardii and C. thalictroides. All Ceratopteris are true ferns: they produce no flowers or seeds, but reproduce vegetatively and by spores.

Description: leaves, stalks and stems are bright light green; stems are thick and slightly darker; leaves are delicate, narrow and lace-like, on thin stalks; there is a central stem with shoots; long roots absorb nutrients and anchor the plant; sporangia contain the spores.

Water Wisteria (Hygrophila difformis) is similar but is a flowering plant with seeds, with slightly broader leaves, more distinct stems with leaves and roots at the nodes, thicker leaves and less bushy growth, and it can change leaf shape (heterophylly). Water Sprite is sturdier, bushier, has thinner leaves and a central growing point.

Uses: attractive mid- or background plant; hiding place for small fish, fry and shrimp (it increases shrimplet survival); takes up nutrients and helps keep nitrate under control; quickly outcompetes most algae. In Madagascar it is eaten as a vegetable, and raw as a salad in Micronesia.

Tankmates: suitable for community tanks with fish, invertebrates and plants. Compatible with plants such as Anacharis, Anubias, Bucephalandra, Cryptocoryne, Hornwort, Java fern and Water Wisteria. Keep with fish such as bettas, tetras, mollies, zebra danios, platies and guppies; snails such as ramshorn, nerite, Malaysian trumpet, Japanese trapdoor and mystery snails (watch snails that nibble the plant); and shrimp such as Neocaridina, Caridina, Amano and ghost shrimp. Do not keep with bamboo or vampire shrimp, whose feeding needs water flow that Water Sprite dislikes. Avoid gouramis, goldfish and herbivorous cichlids, which eat the leaves.

Problems: pale growth indicates iron deficiency; holes in older leaves indicate potassium deficiency; browning leaves are mostly due to poor fertilisation (root tabs can help); algae come from too many nutrients and too much light, so change water regularly, reduce light and trim affected stems; Amano shrimp, nerite snails and Otocinclus can help.

When buying: look for vibrant green leaves and stems, a long, abundant, sturdy root system and a strong upright stem. Avoid pale plants, holes, discolouration, and tears or cuts in the leaves. Quarantine new plants, as they can carry parasites, pest snails or predators such as dragonfly and damselfly nymphs, or be treated with pesticides that are extremely poisonous to shrimp and invertebrates.
